## How to use this

The code from Lecture 15, filled in, with the numbers it produces.

. . .

Optimizers are numerical, so your last decimal place may differ from mine.
Anything beyond that is worth asking about.

::: {.notes}
Posted after class so nobody is left wondering whether their answer was right.
:::

## Setting up

```{r}
bbs <- read.csv("https://github.com/bmaitner/biometry_course/raw/refs/heads/main/data/BBS/FL_BBS.csv")

routes_2019 <- length(unique(bbs$Route[bbs$Year == 2019]))

with_bobwhite <- length(unique(bbs$Route[bbs$Year == 2019 &
                       bbs$Scientific_Name == "Colinus virginianus"]))

bobwhite <- bbs$total_sightings[bbs$Scientific_Name == "Colinus virginianus"]

c(routes = routes_2019, with_bobwhite = with_bobwhite, counts = length(bobwhite))
```

## Trying values of `p` {.smaller}

```{r}
dbinom(x = 52, size = 71, prob = 0.5)
dbinom(x = 52, size = 71, prob = 0.6)
dbinom(x = 52, size = 71, prob = 0.73)
dbinom(x = 52, size = 71, prob = 0.8)
```

The biggest is at `p = 0.73`, and 52/71 = `r round(52/71, 3)`.

::: {.notes}
A result of 52 out of 71 is about 2,900 times more likely under p = 0.73 than
under p = 0.5. That ratio is what likelihood is measuring.
:::

## Why the product fails {.smaller}

```{r}
prod(dpois(bobwhite[1:5], lambda = 10.8))

prod(dpois(bobwhite[1:50], lambda = 10.8))

prod(dpois(bobwhite, lambda = 10.8))
```

The last one is not a small number. It is **zero**: R cannot hold anything below
about `r signif(.Machine$double.xmin, 3)`.

```{r}
sum(dpois(bobwhite, lambda = 10.8, log = TRUE))
```

On the log scale the same quantity is an ordinary number.

## One parameter, fitted {.smaller}

```{r}
binom_nll <- function(p){
  -dbinom(x = with_bobwhite, size = routes_2019, prob = p, log = TRUE)
}

fit <- optimize(binom_nll, interval = c(0, 1))

c(estimate = fit$minimum, nll = fit$objective)
```

Compare with the formula answer:

```{r}
with_bobwhite / routes_2019
```

::: {.notes}
Agreement to four decimals. For a binomial the MLE is provably the sample
proportion, which is why this is a good place to check the machinery.
:::

## Two parameters, fitted {.smaller}

```{r}
nb_nll <- function(mu, size){
  -sum(dnbinom(bobwhite, mu = mu, size = size, log = TRUE))
}

fit_nb <- optim(par = c(mu = 10, size = 1),
                fn = function(p){
                  nb_nll(p["mu"], p["size"])
                },
                method = "BFGS")

round(fit_nb$par, 3)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
mu_m <- mean(bobwhite)
size_m <- mu_m^2 / (var(bobwhite) - mu_m)
knitr::kable(data.frame(method = c("method of moments", "maximum likelihood"),
                        mu = round(c(mu_m, fit_nb$par["mu"]), 3),
                        size = round(c(size_m, fit_nb$par["size"]), 3)))
```

The means agree. The clumping does not, and likelihood is the one to trust.

## Do the two routes agree? {.smaller}

```{r}
library(bbmle)

m1 <- mle2(minuslogl = nb_nll,
           start = list(mu = 10, size = 1),
           data = list(bobwhite = bobwhite))

coef(m1)

coef(m1) - fit_nb$par
```

Zero, because `mle2()` calls `optim()` underneath. A stronger check is to change
the search algorithm:

```{r}
fit_nm <- optim(par = c(mu = 10, size = 1),
                fn = function(p){
                  nb_nll(p["mu"], p["size"])
                },
                method = "Nelder-Mead")

round(fit_nm$par - fit_nb$par, 4)
```

## Estimating the decline {.smaller}

The two pieces you had to supply were the **body of `trend_nll`** and the
**call to it** inside `optim`:

```{r}
bob <- bbs[bbs$Scientific_Name == "Colinus virginianus", ]
counts <- bob$total_sightings
year <- bob$Year - min(bob$Year)

trend_nll <- function(mu0, decline, size){
  mu <- mu0 * (1 - decline)^year
  -sum(dnbinom(counts, mu = mu, size = size, log = TRUE))
}

fit_trend <- optim(par = c(mu0 = 15, decline = 0.03, size = 1),
                   fn = function(p){
                     trend_nll(p["mu0"], p["decline"], p["size"])
                   },
                   method = "L-BFGS-B",
                   lower = c(0.1, -0.5, 0.05),
                   upper = c(100, 0.5, 50))

round(fit_trend$par, 4)
```

## What that answer means {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-width: 6.6
ym <- aggregate(total_sightings ~ Year, data = bob, FUN = mean)
plot(ym$Year, ym$total_sightings, pch = 16, col = "grey30",
     xlab = "year", ylab = "mean count per route")
yrs <- 0:max(year)
lines(min(bob$Year) + yrs,
      fit_trend$par["mu0"] * (1 - fit_trend$par["decline"])^yrs,
      col = "red", lwd = 3)
```

- **`mu0` = 14.8**: expected count per route in 1996
- **`decline` = 0.029**: about **2.9% fewer each year**, against the 3% we
  assumed on Thursday
- **`size` = 1.43**: the clumping, slightly less clumped than the no-trend fit,
  because some of the spread was really the decline

## Was the trend worth fitting? {.smaller}

```{r}
c(no_trend = round(fit_nb$value, 1), with_trend = round(fit_trend$value, 1))
```

The trend improves the fit by about **31** log-likelihood units, and costs one
extra parameter.

. . .

Whether 31 is worth one parameter is **next week's lecture**. The honest answer
today is "almost certainly yes, and here is how we will check".

## Whichever species you picked {.smaller}

Northern Cardinal, as one example:

```{r}
cards <- bbs$total_sightings[bbs$Scientific_Name == "Cardinalis cardinalis"]

nb_nll2 <- function(mu, size){
  -sum(dnbinom(cards, mu = mu, size = size, log = TRUE))
}

fit_card <- optim(par = c(mu = 50, size = 1),
                  fn = function(p){
                    nb_nll2(p["mu"], p["size"])
                  },
                  method = "BFGS")

round(fit_card$par, 3)

round(mean(cards)^2 / (var(cards) - mean(cards)), 3)   # moment estimate of size
```

The two estimates differ, as they did for the bobwhite. **Which one is larger
depends on the species:** cardinals give 2.55 against 1.95, but Northern
Mockingbird gives 1.18 against 1.34, the other way round. There is no rule to
memorize here, only a reason to prefer likelihood.

## What to take away

1. Likelihood is the probability of your data, read as a function of the
   parameters.
2. Logs turn an impossible product into a workable sum.
3. An optimizer finds the parameters that minimize the negative log-likelihood.
4. **Check it**: against a formula where one exists, against a second algorithm,
   and against a plot.

::: {.notes}
Point 4 is the one that keeps people out of trouble in the final project.
:::
